optionalSupplies: A cloth that smells of home
substitutes: No dish towel? Any clean scarf or cloth.
No chew? Skip it and toast with a scratch if they lean in.
title: Beating the Bounds
clue: An old village custom, a dish towel for a banner and four ordinary objects that are about to become very important.
reveal: Parishes once walked their boundary and tapped each marker stone. You do the same for your dog's home, with your dog leading, and write a charter from what they do: one clause per stone, read aloud and signed.
objective: Walk your dog's home patch at their pace, tap four marker stones, then write a three-clause charter from what they did and read it aloud.
instructions: Choose the boundary: the edge of a fully secure yard, or the inside edge of one or two rooms. Choose four ordinary 'boundary stones' such as a plant pot, a chair leg, a corner of a rug and a cushion, and make a parish banner from a dish towel. Have a card and a pen ready.
Secretly slip a small find under one stone: a cloth that smells of home, or a few pieces of their ration. You know where it is; the dog finds it only if they wish.
Bring your dog out on a leash (a loose leash is fine) and let them lead the way, nose down, along the boundary. Carry the banner and follow.

At each stone say 'bound!' and tap it with a finger, then wait as long as the dog wants to sniff. They may skip a stone, cut across, stop or turn back. After each stone, jot two words on the card: 'sniffed long', 'skipped', 'lay down'.
Whichever stone your dog lingers at longest is crowned the Stone of Honor, whether or not the find was there. If they find the hidden treasure, say nothing and just enjoy it.

Write the charter at the last stone. Make three clauses from your notes ('Article One: the plant pot is hereby theirs. Article Two: the rug corner is a place of quiet. Article Three: whatever is under a cushion belongs to the dog'). Read it aloud in your best town-crier voice, then toast: a chew or the find for your dog, a cup of tea for you.

Sign the charter with your name and a drawn paw, then drape the banner over a chair within sight of their bed, out of chewing reach, with the charter pinned beside it. Next year, walk the bounds again and see which stone wins.
twist: The dog writes the law: whatever they do at the stones becomes a clause of their charter, and the stone they linger at longest is crowned the Stone of Honor.
variations: One room: tap four objects around a single room's edge; ideal for a nervous or new dog.
Seated owner: tap the stones as the dog passes by while you remain on a chair.
Puppy: indoor boundary only until your vet clears yard time, and keep it to five minutes.
Anniversary: walk the bounds on the day you brought them home and see which stone they pick this year.
completion: You walked some or all of the boundary and the charter was read. It counts if your dog skips stones or wanders; follow them.
photoIdea: The banner over the chair with your dog resting nearby, or the Stone of Honor with the charter propped beside it.
memoryPrompt: Which stone did your dog choose as the Stone of Honor, and what was Article One?
supplies: Four ordinary objects as boundary stones
Card and pen for the charter
Chew or treat your dog already eats
dietNotes: Chew or ration pieces only if your dog already eats them safely; ask your vet about diet and portions. Skip the food and use a scent cloth if you prefer.
safety: Check the yard fence and keep a leash on: new dogs are likelier to bolt in the first weeks.
Keep the stones too big to swallow, non-toxic and not sharp, and the banner out of chewing reach.
Puppies: yard only once your vet says it is fine, and keep it very short.
